title: Why Large? Tiny LMs & Agents on Edge/Robotics — Cormac Brick, Google

primary.label: Inference & Model Systems
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: Robotics & Embodied
domains.rationale: Edge AI is fundamentally about embodied and device-deployed AI. The talk explicitly covers robotics (Mini v2 robot demo with real-time sign reading and voice interaction on Jetson Nano), IoT device deployment, and edge hardware targets including Raspberry Pi and NPUs.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The techniques and tools discussed (quantization, fine-tuning, LiteRT, MediaPipe) are general-purpose and applicable across many domains beyond robotics, including mobile apps, browser APIs, and consumer electronics.

summary: Cormac Brick, Principal Engineer on Google's AI Edge team, presents a comprehensive talk on deploying AI models at scale on edge devices, arguing that the binding constraint is DRAM cost and availability—not compute. He covers two tiers of edge-deployable models: "small" models (1–4B parameters, e.g., Gemma 2B) requiring 4–8 GB DRAM, and "tiny" models (50M–500M parameters) needing under 2 GB RAM. For small models, he details mixed 2/4/8-bit quantization of Gemma 2B achieving 2.9 bits/weight (~841 MB for weights, ~2 GB active RAM with KV cache), with decode speeds of 7.6 tokens/sec on Raspberry Pi, ~24 on Jetson Nano, and ~31 on Qualcomm IoT NPU. For tiny models, the playbook shifts from zero-shot prompting to fine-tuning with synthetically generated data (10K–10M samples), using base models like Gemma 3 (270M) and Function Gemma. A fine-tuned mobile actions model handles 10 output functions at 86%+ reliability; pairing ASR with it enables voice-to-function calling critical for IoT devices. Production examples include an offline iOS voice dictation app using two sub-billion Gemma models (ASR + text cleanup) and Chrome's built-in summarization/proofreading APIs powered by tiny models. The talk also covers Google's open-source edge AI tool stack (LiteRT-LM, LiteRT, MediaPipe, AI Edge Gallery) and the mobile-actions dataset on Hugging Face. A Mini v2 robot demo illustrates real-time multimodal interaction on Jetson Nano, while Raspberry Pi-based interaction remains too slow for some use cases.
whyItMatters: The concepts in this talk form a coherent engineering framework for deploying AI on resource-constrained devices. The progression is: (1) identify DRAM as the binding constraint, (2) apply mixed-bit quantization to compress models within that constraint, (3) benchmark decode speeds driven by memory bandwidth across device tiers, (4) recognize when even small models are too large, (5) pivot to tiny models with synthetic-data fine-tuning, (6) architect dual-model or voice-to-function pipelines for production use cases, and (7) leverage the open-source LiteRT/MediaPipe stack to implement it all. Software engineering concepts (quantization, KV cache, tool stack, decode speed, model tier selection, dual-model architecture, browser APIs) and AI concepts (tiny LMs, function calling, LoRA, multimodal inference, NPU acceleration, synthetic data pipelines, edge vs cloud trade-offs) are tightly interlinked: the AI capabilities are only deployable because the software engineering techniques make them fit within hardware constraints, and the engineering decisions are driven by the AI model characteristics (parameter count, attention mechanism, data requirements).
temporalContext: This talk was presented at AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 on July 25, 2026. At that time, Gemma 2B and Gemma 3 were the primary edge model families discussed. Since then, Gemma 4 (released April 2026) has superseded these as the latest generation, with E2B and E4B sizes specifically designed for edge deployment under Apache 2.0 license. FunctionGemma 270M was released December 2025. LiteRT-LM was at v0.16.0 as of August 2026. The DRAM cost trend (Raspberry Pi 5 6GB costing 2.5x launch price) was current as of mid-2026. The field of tiny model research remains much less studied than large models, as noted in the talk.
takeaways: DRAM cost and availability, not compute, is the binding constraint for edge AI, worsening as phone makers ship less DRAM and Raspberry Pi 5 6GB costs 2.5x launch price
Small models (1-4B parameters) require 4-8GB DRAM, restricting deployment to laptops, high-end phones, and premium robotics/IoT
Gemma 2B quantized to 2.9 bits/weight needs ~841MB for weights and ~2GB active RAM including KV cache, establishing a 4GB+ device rule of thumb
Tiny models (50M-500M parameters) need less than 2GB RAM, ship natively with apps, and reach older laptops, cheap devices, and background system features
Fine-tuning tiny models with 10K-10M synthetic data samples achieves high reliability, matching or exceeding larger models on specific tasks like function calling at 86%+ accuracy
Decode speeds scale with model size: 7.6 tokens/sec (2B on Raspberry Pi) vs ~45 tokens/sec (tiny model on Raspberry Pi) due to reduced memory reads
Production-ready offline voice dictation app uses two sub-billion Gemma models for ASR and text cleanup, with no subscription required
Voice-to-function calling is a key capability for IoT/edge devices where traditional UI settings menus are challenging for users
Google AI Edge's playbook: develop for first-party use, then share via open-source tools (LiteRT-LM, LiteRT, MediaPipe) and datasets (mobile actions on Hugging Face)
Chrome ships built-in summarization and proofreading APIs powered by tiny models, reaching a wider user base than larger models would allow

concepts.name: Tiny language models (50M–500M parameters)
concepts.explanation: Models in the 50M–500M parameter range that run on devices with less than 2 GB RAM, requiring fine-tuning rather than zero-shot prompting. Base models like Gemma 3 (270M) and Function Gemma serve as starting points.
concepts.importance: These models represent the frontier of accessible AI, reaching older laptops, cheap consumer devices, and background system features where even small models are too large.

concepts.name: Function calling on edge devices
concepts.explanation: Training small models to translate natural language (or voice input) into executable function calls on edge devices. Function Gemma 270M handles 10 mobile actions at 86%+ reliability after fine-tuning.
concepts.importance: Function calling is the bridge between language models and actionable device control, enabling agent-like behavior on constrained hardware.

concepts.name: Quantization to sub-3 bits per weight
concepts.explanation: Using mixed 2-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit quantization plus per-layer embeddings to compress Gemma 2B to 2.9 bits/weight (~841 MB), enabling deployment on 4 GB+ devices.
concepts.importance: Pushing quantization below 3 bits/weight while maintaining model quality is a key enabler for fitting capable models in constrained edge memory.

concepts.name: LoRA adapters for edge deployment
concepts.explanation: Low-Rank Adaptation adapters mentioned as a technique for adapting small models on edge devices, enabling function calling and agent skills without full retraining.
concepts.importance: LoRA provides a parameter-efficient way to specialize models on edge devices, reducing the data and compute needed for adaptation.

concepts.name: On-device multimodal inference
concepts.explanation: Running vision-language models on edge devices, such as Apple's fast VLM (0.5B) on Android with hardware acceleration, or the Mini v2 robot performing real-time sign reading and voice+image interaction on Jetson Nano.
concepts.importance: Multimodal capability on edge hardware broadens the application space from text-only to vision, robotics, and real-time interaction.

concepts.name: NPU-accelerated inference
concepts.explanation: Using neural processing units (NPUs) like Qualcomm IoT NPU to achieve ~4,000 tokens/sec prefill and ~31 tokens/sec decode for 2B models, and higher throughput for tiny models.
concepts.importance: NPUs provide dedicated AI acceleration on edge hardware, significantly improving inference performance and energy efficiency compared to CPU-only execution.

concepts.name: Agent-generated synthetic data pipelines
concepts.explanation: Future ambition where agents generate synthetic training data automatically, reducing the manual effort of creating fine-tuning datasets for tiny models.
concepts.importance: This represents the forward-looking direction for scaling tiny-model development, potentially automating the data pipeline that currently requires significant investment.

concepts.name: Edge AI vs cloud inference trade-offs
concepts.explanation: Edge AI offers low/consistent latency, privacy (data stays on device), offline reliability, and cost savings at scale. Cloud calls become expensive when multiplied by many users.
concepts.importance: Understanding these trade-offs is foundational for deciding whether to deploy on edge or in cloud for a given application.

concepts.name: Mixed-bit model quantization (2/4/8-bit)
concepts.explanation: Applying different quantization bit-widths (2-bit, 4-bit, 8-bit) to different layers of a model, plus per-layer embeddings, to minimize weight footprint while preserving quality. Gemma 2B reaches 2.9 bits/weight, fitting in ~841 MB.
concepts.importance: This is the primary technique that enables small models to fit within tight DRAM constraints on edge devices, directly addressing the binding constraint of the talk.

concepts.name: KV cache memory management
concepts.explanation: Managing the key-value cache footprint during autoregressive decoding, which together with model weights determines the total active RAM. For Gemma 2B, weights are ~841 MB but total active RAM including runtime and KV cache is ~2 GB.
concepts.importance: KV cache is a critical component of total memory budget that is often overlooked when only weight size is considered, and it determines the 4 GB+ device rule of thumb.

concepts.name: Decode speed and memory bandwidth
concepts.explanation: Decode speed (tokens/sec) is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth, not compute. Tiny models read less memory per step, yielding ~45 tokens/sec on Raspberry Pi versus 7.6 for a 2B model, even on the same hardware.
concepts.importance: Explains why smaller models are dramatically faster on the same hardware—reducing memory reads per step is the lever, not increasing compute power.

concepts.name: Synthetic data fine-tuning pipeline
concepts.explanation: Generating 10K–10M synthetic data samples to fine-tune a small base model (e.g., Function Gemma 270M) for a specific task, achieving reliability matching or exceeding larger general-purpose models on that task.
concepts.importance: This is the core playbook for making tiny models viable, replacing zero-shot prompting with task-specific training when off-the-shelf models are insufficient.

concepts.name: Voice-to-function calling architecture
concepts.explanation: Pairing an ASR (automatic speech recognition) model in front of a fine-tuned function-calling model to translate spoken input into executable API actions on edge devices, critical for IoT where traditional UIs are impractical.
concepts.importance: This architecture pattern extends model utility to devices without keyboards or screens, opening a wide range of edge/IoT use cases.

concepts.name: Edge inference tool stack (LiteRT-LM, LiteRT, MediaPipe)
concepts.explanation: Google's open-source stack for edge AI: LiteRT (on-device runtime, successor to TensorFlow Lite), LiteRT-LM (orchestration layer for LLMs on edge), and MediaPipe (cross-platform ML solutions). All maintained under the google-ai-edge GitHub org.
concepts.importance: These are the concrete engineering tools that enable the deployment patterns discussed, and are verified as official Google open-source projects.

concepts.name: Multi-token prediction (MTP) for decode acceleration
concepts.explanation: A technique that increases decode speed by approximately 2x on mobile GPUs by predicting multiple tokens per step. Mentioned as supported by Gemma 4 models via LiteRT-LM.
concepts.importance: MTP is a concrete optimization that further closes the performance gap between edge and cloud inference, making edge deployment more viable.

concepts.name: Dual-model production architecture for offline dictation
concepts.explanation: A production voice dictation app uses two sub-billion Gemma models: one for ASR (speech-to-text) and one for text policing (removing disfluencies, personalization biasing), running fully offline with no subscription.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates that production-quality offline AI experiences are achievable today with tiny models, validating the engineering approach beyond prototypes.

concepts.name: Model tier selection by device RAM budget
concepts.explanation: Choosing between small (1–4B, 4–8 GB DRAM) and tiny (50M–500M, <2 GB RAM) models based on target device memory. Small models use zero-shot prompting; tiny models require fine-tuning.
concepts.importance: This decision framework is the core engineering takeaway for practitioners selecting model sizes for specific hardware targets.

concepts.name: Browser-level AI APIs (Chrome summarization/proofreading)
concepts.explanation: Chrome ships built-in summarization and proofreading APIs powered by tiny models, reaching a wider user base than larger models would allow. These are shipped natively with the browser.
concepts.importance: Shows that tiny models enable AI features in software that serves billions of users where large models would be impractical.

sections.title: Why intelligence at scale needs tiny models
sections.summary: Brick introduces the talk: to put intelligence into many devices, not just expensive robots, we need tiny models. He outlines the agenda covering his background, the AI Edge team, small models' capabilities and limits, and the need for even smaller models.

sections.title: The Google AI Edge team and its open source stack
sections.summary: Brick describes his role as tech lead on Google's AI Edge team, which builds open-source projects (LiteRT-LM, LiteRT, MediaPipe), delivers edge AI core tech to Google products, works with the Gemma team, and focuses on small/tiny models for mobile, browser, and edge deployment. Playbook: develop for first-party use, then share via open source.

sections.title: Why run on the edge at all
sections.summary: Edge AI benefits: low/consistent latency, privacy (data stays on device), offline reliability, and cost savings, especially important at large scale where cheap cloud tokens multiplied by many users add up quickly.

sections.title: The real constraint: DRAM cost
sections.summary: The dominant new challenge is DRAM cost: phone manufacturers ship less DRAM, and Raspberry Pi 5 6GB costs 2.5x launch price. This forces focus on quantization and minimal model sizing. Other challenges include a wide device pool and under-studied small-model research.

sections.title: Small models: 1 to 4 billion parameters
sections.summary: Small models (1-4B) ship in OS-level AI (Android AI Core, Apple Intelligence) and some apps. IoT/robotics typically need 4-8GB DRAM, restricting these models to laptops, high-end phones, and premium electronics. The playbook is mostly zero-shot prompting with LoRA adapters for function calling and agent skills.

sections.title: Shrinking Gemma to 2.9 bits per weight
sections.summary: Gemma 2B is capable at reasoning (on par with much larger models from a year ago). The team uses mixed 2/4/8-bit quantization and per-layer embeddings to achieve 2.9 bits/weight: ~841MB for weights, ~2GB active RAM with KV cache, yielding a 4GB+ device rule of thumb.

sections.title: Decode speeds across Raspberry Pi, Jetson, and NPUs
sections.summary: Using Google's toolchain: Raspberry Pi achieves ~7.6 tokens/sec decode (~2x with MTP), Jetson Nano ~24, Qualcomm IoT NPU ~31 decode with ~4,000 prefill. A high-res image is ~1,120 tokens, so ~3 fps vision is feasible on NPU. Other community models of similar size are also supported.

sections.title: Try it yourself: AI Edge Gallery and a hobby robot
sections.summary: AI Edge Gallery (iOS/Android, fully open source) lets users trial small models on phones. An open-source Mini v2 robot by DeepMind's Zavier demonstrates sign reading, head nodding, and voice+image input; Jetson Nano enables real-time interaction, Raspberry Pi works but slower. For some interactions, even best models do not meet responsiveness requirements.

sections.title: When small is still too big: tiny models
sections.summary: Small models are great when affordable, but too large for older laptops, consumer edge devices, and background system-health AI. This motivates the transition to tiny models, which are introduced next.

sections.title: Off the shelf tiny models: ASR, vision, embeddings
sections.summary: Tiny models range from 50M to 500M parameters, need less than 2GB RAM, and ship natively with applications. Off-the-shelf options include ASR, vision, and embedding models. Apple's fast VLM (0.5B parameters) runs fast on Android with hardware acceleration, providing visual intelligence for edge/IoT devices. Embedding models excel at text processing and matching.

sections.title: Fine tuning for voice to function calling
sections.summary: When off-the-shelf models are insufficient, fine-tuning is the playbook. Base models like Gemma 3 (general purpose) and Function Gemma (function-calling pre-training) start at 270M parameters. Decode jumps to ~45 tokens/sec on Raspberry Pi due to reduced memory reads. A fine-tuned mobile actions model handles 10 output functions at 86%+ reliability from arbitrary text. Pairing ASR in front enables voice-to-function calling, key for IoT devices with challenging UIs. The fine-tuning playbook uses 10K-10M synthetic data samples, with an open-source mobile actions dataset on Hugging Face. This approach matches or exceeds larger model quality on specific tasks while running on far more devices.

sections.title: In production: offline voice dictation
sections.summary: A shipped iOS voice dictation app uses two sub-billion Gemma models, an ASR engine and a text policing engine, that run fully offline with no subscription. It cleans up disfluencies (ums and ahs) and supports personalization biasing toward relevant names and words. Chrome also ships built-in summarization and proofreading APIs powered by tiny models, reaching a wider Chrome user base.

sections.title: Takeaways and Q&A
sections.summary: Key takeaways: small LLMs are easy to use and fast on NPUs; tiny models enable reach to a much larger device pool; voice-to-function calling can be made robust with tiny models using synthetic data fine-tuning. In Q&A, Brick notes future ambitions include generalizing voice-to-function calling, agent-generated synthetic data pipelines, and faster visual models for broader capabilities like segmentation.

organization.name: Google AI Edge
organization.summary: Google AI Edge is Google's end-to-end stack for building and deploying on-device ML and AI across mobile, web, and embedded platforms. The team develops open-source tools including LiteRT-LM (production-ready LLM inference framework for edge devices), LiteRT (on-device ML runtime, successor to TensorFlow Lite), MediaPipe (cross-platform ML solutions), AI Edge Gallery (on-device model trial app), AI Edge Quantizer, and Model Explorer. The team delivers edge AI core technology to Google products (Chrome, Chromebook Plus, Pixel Watch), collaborates with the Google DeepMind Gemma team on model development, and publishes open-source datasets such as the mobile-actions dataset on Hugging Face. The talk's speaker, Cormac Brick, is a Principal Engineer and tech lead on this team. The official developer portal is at ai.google.dev/edge and the open-source repositories are under the github.com/google-ai-edge organization (14 public repos, created November 2023).
organization.status: Active and actively maintained. All major repositories updated within the past month as of August 2026. LiteRT-LM at v0.16.0. Gemma 4 is now the latest model supported by LiteRT-LM. The AI Edge Portal is in private preview for cloud-based benchmarking.

technologies.label: LiteRT Edge Inference Framework
technologies.summary: LiteRT-LM is Google's production-ready, high-performance, open-source inference framework for deploying LLMs on edge devices. The video presents it as the core tool of the AI Edge team, enabling cross-platform deployment (Android, iOS, Web, Desktop, IoT/Raspberry Pi) with GPU/NPU acceleration, function calling, and multi-token prediction (MTP). It sits atop LiteRT (the on-device runtime, successor to TensorFlow Lite) and alongside MediaPipe (cross-platform ML solutions) within the google-ai-edge GitHub ecosystem. The AI Edge Gallery app, built on LiteRT-LM, lets users try models on phones. Verified as actively maintained at v0.16.0 as of August 2026, powering production features in Chrome, Chromebook Plus, and Pixel Watch.
technologies.role: Primary open-source tool stack discussed throughout the talk. The speaker describes these as the AI Edge team's core deliverables, developed for first-party Google use and then shared via open source. LiteRT-LM is the main framework for edge LLM deployment, with LiteRT and MediaPipe as supporting infrastructure.

technologies.label: Gemma Model Family for Edge Deployment
technologies.summary: The Gemma model family is Google DeepMind's open model lineup designed for edge deployment, spanning from small (2B parameter) to tiny (270M parameter) sizes. The video discusses Gemma 2B as the primary small model, quantized to 2.9 bits/weight via mixed 2/4/8-bit quantization, and Gemma 3/Function Gemma at 270M as base models for tiny-model fine-tuning. Function Gemma, specialized for function calling, achieves 86%+ reliability on 10 mobile actions after synthetic-data fine-tuning and powers production voice dictation. Gemma 4 (E2B, E4B), released April 2026 under Apache 2.0, has since superseded earlier generations with the E2B's 841MB footprint matching the talk's cited figures.
technologies.role: The Gemma family is the primary model lineup discussed across both small and tiny model tiers. Gemma 2B exemplifies the small model tier with quantization benchmarks; Function Gemma 270M exemplifies the tiny model tier with fine-tuning for function calling. Production examples use two sub-billion Gemma models for offline voice dictation.

technologies.label: Mixed-Bit Quantization for Edge Model Compression
technologies.summary: Mixed-bit quantization is the primary technique that enables small language models to fit within tight DRAM constraints on edge devices. By applying different bit-widths (2-bit, 4-bit, 8-bit) to different layers plus per-layer embeddings, Gemma 2B is compressed to 2.9 bits/weight (~841MB for weights), while total active RAM including KV cache reaches ~2GB, establishing a 4GB+ device rule of thumb. This technique directly addresses the binding constraint of DRAM cost identified in the talk. Decode speed is bottlenecked by memory bandwidth rather than compute, so smaller quantized models are dramatically faster: 7.6 tokens/sec for 2B on Raspberry Pi vs ~45 tokens/sec for tiny models, because less memory is read per step.
technologies.role: Central engineering technique discussed for enabling edge deployment. The speaker details how mixed 2/4/8-bit quantization plus per-layer embeddings achieves 2.9 bits/weight for Gemma 2B, fitting in ~841MB and ~2GB active RAM. This is presented as the direct response to the DRAM cost constraint that is the talk's central thesis.

technologies.label: Synthetic Data Fine-Tuning for Tiny Edge Models
technologies.summary: Synthetic data fine-tuning is the core playbook for making tiny models (50M-500M parameters) viable on edge devices where zero-shot prompting with larger models is infeasible. The pipeline involves: selecting a base model (Gemma 3 270M or Function Gemma), generating 10K-10M synthetic data samples, and fine-tuning for a specific task. A fine-tuned mobile actions model handles 10 output functions at 86%+ reliability. Pairing an ASR model in front enables voice-to-function calling, critical for IoT devices where traditional UIs are impractical. Production examples include an offline iOS voice dictation app using two sub-billion Gemma models (ASR + text cleanup) and Chrome's built-in summarization/proofreading APIs. Decode jumps to ~45 tokens/sec on Raspberry Pi for tiny models due to reduced memory reads per step.
technologies.role: The fine-tuning playbook is the central engineering topic of the tiny models section of the talk. The speaker presents it as the solution when off-the-shelf models are insufficient, with concrete examples of Function Gemma fine-tuning, the mobile-actions dataset, and shipped production applications.
